Organisation.intro: Multicellular organisms are organised into a hierarchy of increasing complexity. Understanding this hierarchy is essential for B2.
Organisation.mnemonic: Remember the order with: 'Clever Tigers Often Outrun Ordinary Slowpokes' — Cells, Tissues, Organs, Organ systems, Organisms. Or just picture a building: bricks (cells) → walls (tissues) → rooms (organs) → the whole house (organ system) → the neighbourhood (organism).

sections.title: The Hierarchy of Organisation
numbered: Tissues — groups of similar cells working together (e.g. muscle tissue)
Organs — groups of different tissues working together (e.g. stomach)
Organ systems — groups of organs working together (e.g. digestive system)

callout.label: Memory Aid
callout.text: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ System → Organism. Remember: 'C-T-O-O-O' or 'Cells Typically Organise Organisms Outstandingly'.

sections.imageCaption: Hierarchy of biological organisation: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism

sections.title: Examples at Each Level
sections.text: Being able to give examples at each level is a common exam question:
points: Cell example — muscle cell, red blood cell, nerve cell
Tissue example — muscle tissue (many muscle cells), epithelial tissue (lining cells)
Organ example — stomach (muscle tissue + epithelial tissue + nerve tissue)
Organ system example — digestive system (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas)
Organism example — a human being — all organ systems working together

sections.title: Enzymes and the Digestive System
sections.text: The digestive system is a key organ system in B2. Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up digestion:
points: Enzyme — biological catalyst; speeds up reactions; not used up
Active site — specific shape that only fits one substrate (lock and key model)
Optimum temperature — body enzymes work best at ~37°C
Denaturation — irreversible change in enzyme shape caused by high temperature or extreme pH
pH sensitivity — stomach enzymes work best at pH 2; small intestine enzymes at pH 7–8

keyTerms.def: A group of similar cells working together to carry out a specific function
A structure made of different tissues working together to perform a function
A group of organs working together to perform a major function
The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms
A biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions without being used up
The permanent change in shape of an enzyme's active site caused by high temperature or extreme pH, stopping it working
The specific region of an enzyme where the substrate binds

examTips: Know the correct order of the hierarchy — cells are the smallest, organisms the largest.
Be able to give examples at each level: e.g. muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart → cardiovascular system.
In 6-mark questions on organisation, always link structure to function — explain WHY each level is organised as it is.
Enzymes denature above their optimum temperature — the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits. Do not say enzymes are 'killed'.
commonMistakes: Reversing the order of the hierarchy — always go cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organisms.
Confusing a tissue (same cells) with an organ (different tissues working together).
Saying enzymes are 'killed' by heat — the correct term is 'denatured'. Enzymes are proteins, not living things.
clozePassages: Living organisms are organised in a hierarchy from smallest to largest. Cells are the basic unit of life. Groups of similar cells form a tissue. Different tissues working together form an organ. A group of organs working together form an organ system. The digestive system, nervous system, and circulatory system are all examples of organ systems in the human body.

The digestive system is an organ system that breaks down food into small molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. Key organs include the stomach, small intestine, and large intestine. The stomach produces acid and enzymes to begin digestion. The small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption of nutrients into the bloodstream.

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in the body. Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape that only one substrate can fit into — this is called the lock and key model. Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature and pH. If temperature or pH changes too much, the enzyme becomes denatured and stops working.

Digestion.intro: Digestion is the process of breaking down large food molecules into smaller ones that can be absorbed into the bloodstream. Enzymes are key to this process.
Digestion.mnemonic: Remember the three main digestive enzymes with 'APL': Amylase (starch → sugars), Protease (proteins → amino acids), Lipase (lipids → fatty acids + glycerol). Or: 'A Proper Lunch' — A for Amylase, P for Protease, L for Lipase.

sections.title: Enzymes in Digestion
points: Amylase — breaks down starch into sugars; produced in salivary glands and pancreas; works in mouth and small intestine
Protease — breaks down proteins into amino acids; produced in stomach, pancreas, small intestine
Lipase — breaks down fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol; produced in pancreas and small intestine

sections.title: The Digestive System
points: Mouth — mechanical digestion; amylase in saliva begins starch digestion
Oesophagus — moves food to stomach by peristalsis
Stomach — produces HCl (pH 2) to kill bacteria and activate pepsin; protease digestion
Small intestine — main site of digestion and absorption; villi increase surface area
Large intestine — absorbs water; compacts waste into faeces
Liver — produces bile; Pancreas — produces enzymes and sends to small intestine

sections.title: Bile
sections.text: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the small intestine.
points: Emulsifies fats — breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones
This increases the surface area for lipase to work on
Bile is alkaline — neutralises stomach acid in the small intestine
Bile is NOT an enzyme — it does not break down fats chemically

sections.title: Absorption in the Small Intestine
sections.text: The small intestine is highly adapted for absorbing the products of digestion into the blood:
points: Villi — finger-like projections that massively increase surface area for absorption
Microvilli — tiny projections on each villus cell, further increasing surface area
Rich blood supply — maintains a concentration gradient so absorption is rapid
Lacteals — lymph vessels inside villi that absorb fatty acids and glycerol
One cell thick walls — short diffusion distance for rapid absorption of glucose and amino acids

keyTerms.def: A biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions without being used up
Enzyme that breaks down starch into simple sugars
Enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids
Enzyme that breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Alkaline liquid produced by the liver that emulsifies fats
Breaking large fat droplets into smaller droplets to increase surface area
Finger-like projections lining the small intestine that increase surface area for absorption
Wave-like muscle contractions that push food along the digestive tract

examTips: Bile is NOT an enzyme — it physically breaks up fat droplets (emulsification) rather than chemically digesting them.
Know where each enzyme is produced AND where it acts — these are often different places.
The stomach is acidic (HCl); the small intestine is alkaline (bile neutralises the acid).
For 'explain the role of villi' questions, always mention: large surface area, rich blood supply, and thin walls — all three features together maximise absorption.
commonMistakes: Saying bile digests fats — bile only emulsifies (physically breaks up) fats.
Forgetting that amylase works in the mouth as well as the small intestine.
Confusing where enzymes are MADE with where they WORK.
clozePassages: Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates into simple sugars such as glucose. Proteases break down proteins into amino acids. Lipases break down fats into fatty acids and glycerol. These enzymes are produced by glands including the salivary glands, stomach, and pancreas, and work in different parts of the digestive system.

Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the small intestine where it emulsifies fats — breaking large fat droplets into smaller ones. This increases the surface area for lipase enzymes to work on. Bile is alkaline, which also neutralises the acidic contents from the stomach, providing the optimum pH for intestinal enzymes.

The small intestine is the main site of absorption of digested food. Its inner wall is lined with finger-like projections called villi, which increase the surface area for absorption. Each villus has a rich blood supply and contains a lacteal for absorbing fatty acids. The villi also have microvilli on their surface, further increasing surface area.

Heart and Circulation.intro: The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood around the body through a double circulatory system. Understanding its structure and function is key to B2.
Heart and Circulation.mnemonic: To remember blood flow through the heart: 'All Vans Are Cool, People Love Awesome Vehicles' — Atria → Valves → Atria Contract → Pulmonary / Left → Aorta → Ventricles. Simpler: Right side = lungs (Pulmonary), Left side = body (systemic). 'Right is short-haul, Left is long-haul.'

sections.title: Double Circulatory System
points: Pulmonary circulation — heart → lungs → heart (picks up oxygen, drops off CO₂)
Systemic circulation — heart → body → heart (delivers oxygen, picks up CO₂)
The heart acts as a double pump — right side pumps to lungs; left side pumps to body

sections.title: Structure of the Heart
points: 4 chambers: left and right atria (upper), left and right ventricles (lower)
Valves — prevent backflow of blood (atrioventricular valves and semilunar valves)
Left ventricle has thicker walls — pumps blood to the whole body (higher pressure needed)
Right ventricle has thinner walls — pumps blood to the nearby lungs only
Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen

sections.title: Blood Vessels
points: Arteries — carry blood AWAY from the heart; thick muscular walls; high pressure
Veins — carry blood TO the heart; thin walls; low pressure; have valves to prevent backflow
Capillaries — very narrow; walls one cell thick; site of exchange between blood and tissues

sections.title: The Cardiac Cycle and Rate
sections.text: The heart beats in a regular cycle controlled by electrical signals:
points: Sinoatrial node (SAN) — natural pacemaker; sends electrical impulse across atria
Atria contract first — pushing blood into ventricles through atrioventricular valves
Ventricles contract — push blood out to lungs and body through semilunar valves
Artificial pacemaker — fitted under the skin when the SAN is faulty
Resting heart rate — typically 60–100 bpm; lower in trained athletes due to stronger heart muscle

keyTerms.def: Upper chamber of the heart that receives blood
Lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out
Flap in the heart or vein that prevents backflow of blood
Blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure
Blood vessel that carries blood towards the heart at low pressure
Tiny blood vessel with walls one cell thick where exchange occurs
The heart's natural pacemaker — generates electrical impulses to control heartbeat
The circuit of blood between the heart and the lungs

examTips: Left ventricle has thicker walls than right — it pumps blood the full length of the body.
Arteries ALWAYS carry blood away from the heart (even pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs).
Veins have valves; arteries do not (they rely on high pressure).
In questions about heart structure, always connect wall thickness to the distance blood must travel — left = whole body = thicker walls.
commonMistakes: Saying arteries always carry oxygenated blood — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.
Confusing atria and ventricles — atria receive blood, ventricles pump it out.
Forgetting why the left ventricle has thicker walls.
clozePassages: The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood around the body. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, while the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. This is called the double circulatory system. The heart has four chambers: two atria at the top and two ventricles at the bottom.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure and have thick, muscular walls. Veins carry blood back to the heart under low pressure and have valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries are tiny vessels with walls one cell thick, allowing exchange of substances between the blood and body tissues. The network of blood vessels is called the circulatory system.

The heart rate is controlled by a group of cells called the sinoatrial node (SAN), which acts as a natural pacemaker. It sends electrical impulses that cause the atria to contract, then the ventricles. If the natural pacemaker is faulty, an artificial pacemaker can be fitted. Heart valves prevent the backflow of blood and ensure it flows in the correct direction.

Blood.intro: Blood is a tissue made up of several components, each with a specific function. Understanding these components is essential for B2.
Blood.mnemonic: Remember the four components of blood with 'PRWP': Plasma, Red blood cells, White blood cells, Platelets. Or use the silly phrase 'Pretty Red Wolves Play' — Plasma (pretty yellow), Red blood cells, White blood cells (wolves — defenders!), Platelets (play — they patch up wounds).

sections.title: Components of Blood
points: Red blood cells — contain haemoglobin; carry oxygen; biconcave disc shape; no nucleus (more room for haemoglobin)
White blood cells — part of the immune system; fight infection; phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies
Platelets — small cell fragments; trigger blood clotting at wounds
Plasma — yellow liquid; transports: digested food, CO₂, urea, hormones, heat

sections.title: Red Blood Cells
sections.text: Red blood cells are highly adapted for carrying oxygen:
points: Biconcave disc shape — increases surface area for oxygen absorption
No nucleus — more space for haemoglobin
Flexible — can squeeze through narrow capillaries
Haemoglobin + O₂ → oxyhaemoglobin (in lungs)
Oxyhaemoglobin → haemoglobin + O₂ (at body tissues)

sections.title: Plasma and Platelets
sections.text: Plasma is the liquid component of blood; platelets help seal wounds:
points: Plasma composition — water (~90%), dissolved substances including glucose, amino acids, CO₂, urea, hormones, and heat
CO₂ transport — most CO₂ is carried dissolved in plasma (some in red blood cells as carbonic acid)
Urea transport — urea produced in liver from amino acid breakdown is carried in plasma to kidneys
Platelets trigger clotting — a cascade of reactions produces fibrin, a protein mesh that traps red blood cells to form a clot
Scab formation — the clot dries to form a scab, preventing pathogen entry

keyTerms.def: Red protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen
White blood cell that engulfs and destroys pathogens
White blood cell that produces antibodies
Liquid component of blood that transports dissolved substances
Cell fragments that help blood clot at wounds
The compound formed when haemoglobin combines with oxygen in the lungs
A protein produced during clotting that forms a mesh to trap red blood cells and seal wounds

examTips: Red blood cells have no nucleus — this is an adaptation allowing more haemoglobin and therefore more oxygen carried.
Plasma transports many things — CO₂, urea, hormones, glucose, amino acids, heat.
Know the two types of white blood cells: phagocytes (engulf) and lymphocytes (antibodies).
When explaining red blood cell adaptations, always link each feature to its function — e.g. 'biconcave shape increases surface area, so more oxygen can be absorbed in a shorter time'.
commonMistakes: Saying red blood cells carry carbon dioxide — they mainly carry oxygen (CO₂ is mostly carried in plasma).
Forgetting that platelets are cell fragments, not whole cells.
Confusing phagocytes and lymphocytes.
clozePassages: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to body tissues. They contain haemoglobin which binds to oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin. White blood cells defend the body against infection by engulfing pathogens or producing antibodies. Platelets are small cell fragments that help blood to clot at wound sites, preventing excessive blood loss.

Plasma is the liquid component of blood, making up about 55% of its volume. It carries red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets around the body. Plasma also transports dissolved substances including glucose, hormones, urea, and carbon dioxide. It plays a key role in distributing heat generated by respiration throughout the body.

Blood clotting is an important defence mechanism. When a blood vessel is damaged, platelets clump together at the site. A series of chemical reactions produces fibrin, a protein that forms a mesh across the wound. This mesh traps red blood cells to form a clot, which dries to form a scab. This prevents pathogens from entering and blood from being lost.

Heart Disease.intro: Coronary heart disease is one of the most common diseases in the UK. Understanding its causes, symptoms, and treatments is important for B2.
Heart Disease.mnemonic: Remember the risk factors for heart disease with 'SHOD FO': Smoking, High blood pressure, Obesity, Diet (high fat), Family history, Old age. And treatments: 'SSB' — Statins, Stents, Bypass surgery.

sections.title: Coronary Heart Disease (CHD)
sections.text: CHD occurs when fatty deposits (plaques) build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.
points: Fatty deposits = atherosclerosis
Reduced blood flow → less oxygen to heart muscle
Can cause angina (chest pain) or heart attack
Risk factors: smoking, high fat diet, lack of exercise, obesity, high blood pressure, genetics

sections.title: Treatments
points: Statins — drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels, slowing plaque build-up
Stents — metal mesh tubes inserted into arteries to keep them open
Bypass surgery — a healthy blood vessel is used to reroute blood around the blocked artery
Artificial heart valves — replace damaged valves; can be mechanical or biological

sections.title: Lifestyle Changes
points: Stop smoking — nicotine raises blood pressure; CO reduces oxygen in blood
Reduce saturated fat intake — lowers LDL cholesterol
Regular exercise — strengthens heart muscle, reduces blood pressure
Maintain healthy weight — reduces strain on heart

sections.title: Evaluating Treatments
sections.text: AQA often asks you to evaluate treatments — weigh up risks and benefits:
points: Statins — benefit: reduce cholesterol long-term, reduce heart attack risk; risk: side effects (muscle pain), must be taken daily for life
Stents — benefit: quick, minimally invasive, immediate improvement; risk: infection, blood clots around stent
Bypass surgery — benefit: restores full blood flow, long-lasting; risk: major surgery with anaesthetic risk, long recovery
Lifestyle changes — benefit: no side effects, improve overall health; limitation: require willpower and sustained behaviour change

keyTerms.def: Blood vessels that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood
Build-up of fatty deposits (plaques) in artery walls, narrowing the lumen
Drug used to lower blood cholesterol levels
A mesh tube inserted into a narrowed artery to keep it open
Chest pain caused by restricted blood flow to the heart muscle
Occurs when a coronary artery is completely blocked, depriving heart muscle of oxygen
A fatty substance in blood that contributes to plaque formation in arteries

examTips: Statins reduce cholesterol — they slow plaque build-up but don't remove existing plaques.
Stents keep arteries open mechanically; bypass surgery creates a new route for blood flow.
Be able to evaluate treatments — consider risks vs benefits.
In 'evaluate' questions, give at least one benefit AND one risk for each treatment mentioned, then justify a conclusion.
commonMistakes: Saying statins dissolve plaques — they only prevent new ones forming by reducing cholesterol.
Confusing coronary arteries (supply the heart) with pulmonary arteries (go to lungs).
Forgetting to mention that coronary heart disease affects the heart MUSCLE'S blood supply — not the blood inside the heart.
clozePassages: Coronary heart disease occurs when the coronary arteries that supply the heart muscle become narrowed by a build-up of fatty deposits called plaques. This restricts blood flow and can cause chest pain called angina. If a coronary artery becomes completely blocked, a heart attack occurs. Risk factors include high blood pressure, smoking, and a high-fat diet.

Coronary heart disease can be treated with stents, which are small metal tubes inserted into narrowed arteries to keep them open. Statins are drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels and slow the build-up of fatty deposits. In severe cases, a heart bypass operation uses blood vessels from elsewhere in the body to route blood around the blocked coronary artery.

Heart failure occurs when the heart cannot pump blood effectively around the body. It can be treated with a heart transplant using a donor heart, or with a mechanical heart as a temporary measure while waiting for a transplant. Valves can also become damaged and may need to be replaced with biological valves from pigs or cows, or with mechanical valves.

Cancer.intro: Cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division. Understanding the difference between benign and malignant tumours, and the risk factors for cancer, is required for B2.
Cancer.mnemonic: Remember the difference: 'Benign = Boring (stays in one place). Malignant = Moves (metastasises).' Or think: Malignant starts with M, just like Metastasis and Moving — malignant tumours MOVE to other parts of the body.

sections.title: What is Cancer?
sections.text: Cancer occurs when mutations in the genes that control cell division cause cells to divide uncontrollably, forming a mass called a tumour.
points: Mutations can be caused by: carcinogens (e.g. chemicals in cigarettes), radiation (UV, X-rays), some viruses
Some cancers are linked to inherited genetic mutations

sections.title: Benign vs Malignant Tumours
points: Benign tumour — stays in one place, does not invade other tissues, not cancerous, usually not life-threatening
Malignant tumour — cancerous; cells break away and spread via blood/lymph to other organs (metastasis); life-threatening

callout.label: Key Distinction
callout.text: Benign = stays put. Malignant = spreads (metastasises). Only malignant tumours are truly cancer.

sections.title: Risk Factors for Cancer
sections.text: Risk factors increase the probability of developing cancer but do not guarantee it:
points: Smoking — chemicals in cigarette smoke are carcinogens; strongly linked to lung cancer
UV radiation — from the sun; damages DNA in skin cells; causes melanoma (skin cancer)
Viral infections — HPV (human papillomavirus) is linked to cervical cancer
Ionising radiation — X-rays and gamma rays can damage DNA
Inherited mutations — BRCA1 gene mutation increases breast and ovarian cancer risk; shows genetic factors matter
Alcohol — linked to liver, mouth, and throat cancer

sections.title: Cancer Treatments
sections.text: Several treatments are used depending on the type and stage of cancer:
points: Surgery — physically removes the tumour; most effective when cancer has not spread
Radiotherapy — targeted ionising radiation kills cancer cells by damaging their DNA
Chemotherapy — drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells; side effects because healthy cells are also affected
Side effects of treatment — hair loss, nausea, and fatigue because treatments affect all rapidly dividing cells, not just cancer cells

keyTerms.def: A mass of abnormal cells formed by uncontrolled cell division
A tumour that remains in one location and does not spread
A cancerous tumour whose cells spread to other parts of the body
The spread of cancer cells from the primary tumour to other parts of the body
A substance that causes cancer by mutating DNA
Use of ionising radiation to destroy cancer cells
Drug treatment targeting rapidly dividing cells to kill cancer

examTips: Always distinguish between benign (non-spreading) and malignant (spreading/cancer) tumours.
Cancer = uncontrolled mitosis due to DNA mutations.
For 'explain why chemotherapy causes side effects' — it kills rapidly dividing healthy cells too, such as hair follicle cells and gut lining cells.
Risk factors increase the CHANCE of cancer — they do not mean cancer will definitely develop.
commonMistakes: Saying all tumours are cancer — only malignant tumours are cancerous.
Forgetting that cancer is caused by mutations in cell division genes, not just any mutation.
Confusing risk factor with cause — having a risk factor does not guarantee you will get cancer.
clozePassages: Cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division resulting in the formation of a tumour. Benign tumours grow in one place and do not spread to other tissues. Malignant tumours can invade and destroy surrounding tissue and spread through the blood to form secondary tumours elsewhere — a process called metastasis. Both lifestyle and genetic factors can increase the risk of cancer.

Risk factors for cancer include smoking, which is strongly linked to lung cancer, exposure to UV radiation from the sun which can cause skin cancer, and certain viral infections such as HPV which is linked to cervical cancer. Inherited faulty genes can also increase risk. Regular screening such as mammograms and smear tests can help detect cancer early when it is most treatable.

Cancer can be treated by radiotherapy, which uses ionising radiation to kill cancer cells. Chemotherapy uses drugs that target rapidly dividing cells. Surgery can physically remove a tumour. These treatments can have side effects because they also affect healthy cells. Early detection through screening programmes significantly improves the chances of successful treatment.

Plant Organisation.intro: Plants are also organised into tissues and organs. The leaf is the main organ for photosynthesis and understanding its structure is important for B2.
Plant Organisation.mnemonic: Remember the two transport tissues with 'X marks the spot for water' — Xylem carries water (X = water). Phloem carries food (Phloem = Food). Or: 'eXit water up Xylem; food Flows in Phloem'. For factors increasing transpiration: 'HoT Wind Lights up' — Higher temperature, airflow (wind), Taller light intensity.

sections.title: Plant Tissues
points: Epidermal tissue — covers the outer surface of leaves and stems; waxy cuticle reduces water loss
Palisade mesophyll — packed with chloroplasts; main site of photosynthesis
Spongy mesophyll — air spaces for gas exchange; some photosynthesis
Xylem — transports water and mineral ions up from roots; dead cells forming hollow tubes
Phloem — transports dissolved sugars (sucrose) from leaves to rest of plant

sections.title: The Leaf
sections.text: The leaf is the main photosynthetic organ, adapted to maximise light absorption and gas exchange:
points: Broad flat surface — maximises light absorption
Thin — short diffusion distance for gases
Many stomata (mainly lower surface) — allow CO₂ in and O₂ out
Stomata controlled by guard cells — open in light, close in dark

sections.title: Transpiration
sections.text: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves through stomata. It drives water up through xylem.
points: Factors that increase transpiration: higher temperature, lower humidity, wind, more light
Measured using a potometer (measures water uptake as a proxy for transpiration)

sections.title: Translocation vs Transpiration
sections.text: These two processes are frequently confused — know the distinction clearly:
points: Transpiration — loss of water vapour from leaves through stomata; drives water UP through xylem
Translocation — transport of dissolved sugars in phloem; can go UP or DOWN the plant
Xylem cells are dead — hollow tubes strengthened with lignin; water moves by cohesion
Phloem cells are alive — have companion cells to supply energy for active loading of sugars
Source to sink — sugars move from where they are made (leaves) to where they are used (roots, fruits, growing points)

keyTerms.def: Plant tissue that transports water and mineral ions upwards from roots
Plant tissue that transports sugars from leaves to the rest of the plant
The loss of water vapour from leaves through the stomata
Tiny pores in leaves that allow gas exchange and water vapour to escape
Cells that surround stomata and control their opening and closing
The transport of dissolved sugars through phloem from leaves to other parts of the plant
Layer of tightly packed cells near the top of a leaf, rich in chloroplasts, main site of photosynthesis
Waterproof layer on the upper surface of leaves that reduces water loss by evaporation

examTips: Xylem transports water UP; phloem transports sugars (translocation) both up and down.
Transpiration is affected by temperature, humidity, wind speed and light intensity.
Stomata open in light (photosynthesis needs CO₂) and close in dark or when water is scarce.
In potometer experiments, the bubble moves because water is taken up by the plant — it measures water uptake, not transpiration directly.
commonMistakes: Saying phloem transports water — it transports sugars. Xylem transports water.
Forgetting that xylem cells are dead (their walls form hollow tubes).
Confusing transpiration (water loss) with translocation (sugar transport in phloem).
clozePassages: Plants have specialised tissues including xylem and phloem. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves in a one-way flow. Phloem transports dissolved sugars made by photosynthesis up and down the plant to where they are needed — a process called translocation. Both tissues form continuous tubes called vascular bundles running throughout the plant.

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves through tiny pores called stomata. This loss of water draws more water up through the xylem from the roots. Transpiration is faster in warm, dry, and windy conditions. Each stoma is controlled by two guard cells which open and close the pore depending on light levels and water availability.

Leaves are adapted for photosynthesis. They have a large, flat surface area to absorb sunlight. The upper surface has a waxy cuticle to reduce water loss. The palisade mesophyll layer contains many chloroplasts and is positioned near the top of the leaf where light is brightest. The spongy mesophyll has air spaces that allow gases to diffuse to and from the cells.
